Aristotle defines the soul as “the first actuality of a natural, organized body capable of life” (2, 412b 5). In Aristotle, form plays the role of actuality—or completion—in relation to matter, which remains only potentially existent until form brings its existence into actuality (Aristotle, 12, 1069b 34). Richard Walzer supports our view that when al-Kindī speaks of the soul as “form,” he means the term in Aristotle’s sense. Walzer says that al-Kindī “refers to Aristotle’s definition of the soul as the form of the body or the completion of the body” (Walzer, Islamic Philosophy and Its Place in Human Thought, trans. Tawfīq Ḥusayn, p. 41).↩︎

This conclusion is confirmed by another passage from al-Kindī himself, in his treatise on “the prostration of the outermost body” (Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 247), where he says: “Form is not separate from its element; the two are united....”↩︎

We think that the treatises addressed to unnamed individuals were probably written to al-Kindī’s students, for two reasons. First, the openings use the tone of a teacher addressing someone who has asked him for knowledge. At the start of the Treatise on the Intellect, for example, al-Kindī says: “I understood what you asked me to set down concerning my account of the intellect” (Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 353). Second, al-Kindī uses the same tone in two treatises that explicitly name men known to have been his students. One is Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Khurāsānī; see al-Kindī’s Treatise Explaining the Finitude of the Body of the World, Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 185; and Father McCarthy, p. 63, no. 111. Ibn al-Nadīm (The Fihrist, p. 261) says that this man was better known as Aḥmad ibn al-Ṭayyib, that he studied under al-Kindī and learned from him, that he later taught the caliph al-Muʿtaḍid (279–289 AH/892–901 CE), and that he was killed in 286 AH/899 CE; see Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, Classes of Physicians, vol. 1, p. 214. The second student whom al-Kindī names is ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm; see Al-Kindī’s Treatise to ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm on the Oneness of God and the Finitude of the Body of the World, Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 201; and Father McCarthy, p. 48, no. 291. This ʿAlī ibn al-Jahm is the well-known Abbasid poet who praised the caliph al-Mutawakkil, was exiled by him in 232 AH, and died in 249 AH. The sources name other students of al-Kindī as well, including Ḥasanawayh, Nafṭawayh, Salmawayh, Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm Quwayrī, and Ibn Karnīb. See Ibn al-Nadīm, The Fihrist, p. 412; and al-Ahwānī, Al-Kindī, Philosopher of the Arabs, p. 77.↩︎

Al-Kindī, Treatise on the Intellect (Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 353). At the opening of this treatise, al-Kindī writes: “... I understood what you asked me to set down concerning the intellect: a brief account of my view, following the opinion of the most highly regarded of the ancient Greeks, foremost among them Aristotle and his teacher, the sage Plato, since Plato’s position on this matter amounted to the position of his pupil Aristotle.” As this passage clearly shows, al-Kindī states that Plato and Aristotle agree in their theory of the intellect. On that basis, he then goes on to present Aristotle’s theory rather than Plato’s, despite the difference between the two theories.↩︎

The section of this treatise dealing with universals, species, and the rational soul can be found in Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 155, or in al-Ahwānī’s edition of Al-Kindī’s Book to al-Muʿtaṣim, p. 134. The passage reads: “The soul becomes actually intelligent when the species unite with it; before they unite with it, it is intelligent only potentially. Anything that exists potentially is brought into actuality by something else that is itself actual in the respect in which it brings the other from potentiality to actuality. What brings the soul, which is potentially intelligent, into actual intelligence is the union with it of the species and genera of things—that is, their universals, and these are the universals of their individual realities [this is the reading in al-Ahwānī’s edition; Abū Rīda’s edition reads: ‘Are universals their individual realities?’]. Through their union with the soul, the soul becomes intelligent—that is, it possesses an intellect, namely the universals of things. The universals of things, when present in the soul and brought from potentiality into actuality, are the soul’s acquired intellect, which it possessed only potentially, through the actual intellect that brought the soul from potentiality into actuality. Since universals are many, intellect is many....”↩︎

The three kinds of intellect that can be drawn from Aristotle’s discussion in On the Soul are: 1. an intellect whose nature is to make all things actual—the active intellect; 2. an intellect that becomes all things—the potential intellect; and 3. the habitual intellect, the human intellect when it is actual. Aristotle illustrates this last state with the example of a learned person who has acquired knowledge and can use it immediately whenever he wishes. This kind of intellect therefore stands between potentiality and actuality: it is actual because the person truly possesses the knowledge, but potential because at a given moment he may not be actively using it. See Aristotle, 3, 430a 10–19; 430a 16; 429b 1–5. Alexander of Aphrodisias, one of the leading commentators on Aristotle between the second and third centuries CE, also divided intellect into three kinds: 1. the material intellect (intellectus materialis), which is intellect in potentiality; 2. an intellect that understands—that is, an actual intellect possessing a settled capacity for understanding (intellectus qui intelligit et habet habitum ut intelligat), so that it can exercise this ability whenever it wishes; and 3. the active intellect (intelligentia agens), an external agent that gives intelligibility to the human intellect and to intelligible forms. Its relation to the potential intellect in the soul is like the relation of light to the eye. In Alexander’s view, this active intellect is necessary for the union of the material intellect with the intelligible form, bringing the intellect from potentiality into actuality. A section of Alexander of Aphrodisias’s On the Soul was translated into Latin as a separate treatise entitled De intellectu et intellecto (“On the Intellect and the Intelligible”). See Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Hādī Abū Rīda, introduction to al-Kindī’s Treatise on the Intellect, in Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, pp. 320–321.↩︎
Aristotle also recognizes these two states. See On the Soul, 2, 417a 22 ff.↩︎

Aristotle devotes chapters 4 and 5 of Book XIII of the Metaphysics to discussing Plato’s theory of Forms. If we look especially at the discussion in chapter 5, we can see that Aristotle rejects separating the universal, which can be grasped by the intellect, from the sensory world. He also rejects a metaphysical separation—in the sense opposed to a dialectical one—between essence and appearance. And he rejects treating the universal as independent of the particular, as though the universal could exist outside particular things. From these aspects of Aristotle’s criticism of Plato’s theory of Forms, Lenin drew the conclusion expressed in his Philosophical Notebooks: Aristotle’s criticism is directed not only against Plato, but against idealism in general.↩︎
Lenin says that there can be no doubt about “the reality of the external world [in Aristotle]” (Philosophical Notebooks, French ed., 1955, p. 287).↩︎

Aristotle may appear to be a sensualist when he stresses this point. But he distances himself from sensualism in On the Soul (2, 417b 22), where he makes clear that although knowledge begins with the senses, it is not formed from sensation and experience alone. He says that science is knowledge of the universal, not the particular, while actual sense perception deals only with individual things—the particulars—and “science concerns the universal.” Here we have used the Arabic text of On the Soul, translated by Isḥāq ibn Ḥunayn, Badawī ed., p. 43. In the Philosophical Notebooks, Lenin likewise rejected the charge of “sensualism” against Aristotle, calling him a thoughtful sensualist in contrast to crude sensualists.↩︎
In On the Soul, Aristotle stresses that the senses do not produce sensation unless they are affected by an object.↩︎

Following Greek philosophical terminology, al-Kindī also calls the “image-forming faculty” by the Greek word phantasia. Majid Fakhry translates it as “imagination” (Majid Fakhry, Aristotle, the First Teacher, Beirut, Catholic Press, 1955, p. 66), while Abū Rīda translates it as “the imaginative faculty” (Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 293). In Aristotle, imagination—or phantasia—occupies an intermediate stage between sensation and thought in the process of abstraction, or thinking (Aristotle, On the Soul, 3, 431a 16).↩︎

See al-Kindī’s Treatise Explaining the Proximate Efficient Cause of Generation and Corruption (Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, pp. 214–237). In this treatise he builds his logical arguments on the assumption that what a proximate cause does is a real, actual, tangible event, not something merely figurative. He says, for example, that motion produces heat in the elements and in things composed of them, and that the elements are affected by motion or by contact. Here motion is an efficient cause of heat. Motion is a real material fact, and heat is a real material fact. The first causes the second, and the cause itself is therefore real and material. What sense, then, does it make to call it merely a figurative cause?↩︎

Al-Kindī expressed his firm scientific belief in the law of causal relations in especially clear and forceful terms when he wrote: “There is nothing in nature that is pointless or without purpose.” See his Treatise Explaining the Prostration of the Outermost Body, Al-Kindī’s Philosophical Treatises, vol. 1, p. 253.↩︎

Al-Fārābī defines philosophy as “knowledge of existing things insofar as they exist” (The Harmonization of the Opinions of the Two Sages, Beirut, 2nd ed., ed. The ideological character of philosophy—of every philosophy—is an objective fact. It does not depend on whether the philosopher is aware of it, nor on whether we recognize it in one philosopher or another. Like every other form of human consciousness, philosophy has no history separate from the history of real people living under particular economic and social conditions. In every society and every age, philosophy therefore presents a system of ideas about the world in which the character of the prevailing social relations and the ideological struggle within those relations are indirectly reflected. Through these ideas, philosophy also defines each philosopher’s position within that struggle.↩︎

Medieval Arab philosophers knew the work called Theology as The Theology of Aristotle or Aristotle’s Book of Divinity. The mistaken attribution to Aristotle may have arisen because the work, whose author was then unknown, reached them together with explanations by Porphyry of Tyre, whom they knew as a commentator on Aristotle. They therefore assumed that the work itself was by Aristotle. ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nāʿima al-Ḥimṣī (d. 220 AH/835 CE) translated it into Arabic, and al-Kindī revised the translation. Dieterici first published it in Berlin in 1882, and it was translated into Latin in 1519. In reality, the work is drawn from the Fourth and Sixth Enneads of Plotinus. See ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī’s edition of the Fourth Ennead, On the Soul, Cairo, 1970, pp. 156–157.↩︎

The Arabic historical sources that record the translation movement under the early and later Abbasids all testify to this. Examples include Ibn al-Nadīm’s Fihrist (pp. 263, 348, 411), al-Qifṭī’s Accounts of the Scholars (pp. 118, 122, 130, 266, and elsewhere), and Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa’s Classes of Physicians (vol. 1, p. 235; vol. 2, p. 335, and elsewhere). Modern historians and researchers—Arab, Eastern, and Orientalist alike—have likewise reached the conclusion, through their studies and textual research, that this historical fact is sound: the Arab philosophers knew Aristotle’s philosophy.↩︎
